questions.solution: Using the quotient rule, f'(x) = [(u(4x - 2))v'(3x^2 + 5x - 7) - u'(3x^2 + 5x - 7)v(4x - 2)] / v(4x - 2)^2, where u(x) = 3x^2 + 5x - 7 and v(x) = 4x - 2. So, u'(x) = 6x + 5 and v'(x) = 4. Plugging these into the formula gives us f'(x) = [(6x + 5)(4) - (3x^2 + 5x - 7)(-2)] / (4x - 2)^2.
questions.explanation: The quotient rule is used to differentiate functions that are in the form of a ratio of two functions. The common mistake is forgetting to square the denominator in the denominator of the fraction.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Forgetting to square the denominator (4x - 2)^2 leads to choice A.

questions.stem: Find the derivative of g(x) = (e^x + sin(x))/(cos(x)).
questions.solution: Using the quotient rule, g'(x) = [(u(cos(x))v'(e^x + sin(x)) - u'(e^x + sin(x))v(cos(x))) / v(cos(x))^2], where u(x) = e^x + sin(x) and v(x) = cos(x). So, u'(x) = e^x + cos(x) and v'(x) = -sin(x). Plugging these into the formula gives us g'(x) = [(e^x + cos(x)(-sin(x)) - (e^x + sin(x))(-sin(x))) / (cos(x))^2].
questions.explanation: The quotient rule is applied to functions in the form of a ratio. A common mistake would be to forget that the derivative of sine is cosine and the derivative of cosine is negative sine, leading to choice B.
questions.common_mistake_notes: Forgetting the derivatives of sine and cosine leads to choice B.

So, u'(x) = 3x^2 + 2 and v'(x) = 10x. Plugging these into the formula gives us h'(x) = [(x^3 + 2x)(10x) - (3x^2 + 2)(10x)] / (5x^2 - 1)^2.
